quotes.text: Microservices pay off later, not early. For teams under roughly 20 to 30 engineers, the coordination cost often beats the scaling benefit. You don't get independence. You get dependency with more steps.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Sums up when microservices stop paying off for small teams.

quotes.text: Strong governance can help velocity, but only when it behaves like infrastructure and not committee process.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear rule for automated rather than manual governance.

quotes.text: If you can't answer that in one sentence, the safest default is usually to keep the capability in process and design the boundary inside the code first.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: A modular monolith is not one giant shared mess, but rather one deployable with rules. The extraction path stays open later because the capability boundary already exists
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Corrects the misconception that a monolith must be unstructured.

quotes.text: If those numbers are getting worse, while the diagram gets cleaner, the diagram is lying to you.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Memorable call to judge architecture by delivery outcomes.

chapters.title: The hidden tax of distributed complexity
API contracts as digital red tape

takeaways: Microservices add network, observability, mesh and coordination costs that often outweigh their benefits for smaller teams.
Rigid API contracts and manual governance turn into digital red tape; move checks into CI and pull requests instead.
Default to a modular monolith with clear internal boundaries and separate services only when a concrete problem requires it today.
hook: Microservices promised speed, but many .NET teams now spend more time on contracts, tracing and coordination than on features. This episode explains the hidden costs of distributed architectures and gives architects and engineering leads a practical model for deciding what should be a service and what should stay a module.
